courses.title: Win the won game
courses.sub: Seven short habits for the moment you are winning, so that winning positions become wins.
courses.why: In your 175 analysed games you reached a winning position in 108 and won 74 of them. "Threw away a win" is your most common mistake: 91 times. This is the most common way 1400 players lose won games, and it is the easiest rating to win back.

chapters.title: Converting an advantage
chapters.intro: Seven lessons, one rule each. The examples are moments from your own games where the win slipped away. The cards are your own positions too.

stillgame.title: Winning is not won
stillgame.goal: Keep asking about his threats when you are ahead.
stillgame.rule: When you are ahead, your first question is still: what is his threat?
stillgame.intro: When you are winning, it is natural to relax and look only at your own plans. That is exactly when his one trick works. Before each move, look at his pieces first: what can he check, capture or attack next? Then make your move.

steps.setting: Your game against yanis4dja, 19 Mar 2026. Your queen is stronger than his rook and bishop. You played ((37.g4)) after 3 seconds.

trade.title: Trade pieces, keep pawns
trade.goal: Make the win simpler by swapping pieces when you are ahead.
trade.rule: Ahead in material: swap pieces (not pawns), every fair trade makes the win simpler.
trade.intro: When you are a piece up, every trade of equal pieces makes your extra piece count for more. Fewer pieces also means fewer tricks for him. So when he offers a fair trade, usually take it. Keep your pawns: they are what you will promote in the end.

steps.setting: Your game against matteoborgio, 28 Dec 2025. You are Black with an extra pawn. Watch where his king goes.

Swap the rooks. In the game you played ((37...Rb1)) and most of your advantage was gone.
With one rook each gone, your g-pawn runs, and his rook is too far away to stop it.

steps.keyText: When he offers a trade and you are ahead, take it unless it costs you something.

steps.setting: Your game against Alaa93Salman, 18 Apr 2026. You are White. Black offers to trade queens.

moves.c: He offers the trade, but look: his bishop on f2 is attacked by your rook on f1.
Take the trade.
With the queens gone, the bishop falls as well. Three pawns up with no queens on the board is an easy win.

steps.keyText: A queen trade when you are ahead takes away his best attacker and his tricks.

counterplay.title: Kill his counterplay first
counterplay.goal: Stop his one active idea before you go after more.
counterplay.rule: Before you win more, take away his only active idea: the open file, the passed pawn, the attack on your king.
counterplay.intro: When you are winning, he usually has just one hope: a passed pawn, a rook on your back rank or checks against your king. Find that one idea and stop it. After that, your extra material wins by itself.

steps.setting: Your game against JHSistemas, 20 Feb 2026. You are a rook up, but his pawn on c2 is one step from a new queen. You played ((49.Rd5)) after 3 seconds.

moves.c: His only hope is the c-pawn. After ((49.Rd5 Re1+ 50.Kf2 c1=Q)) he gets a new queen. Check first, then your rook stands behind the pawn.
Your king attacks his rook and comes towards the pawn.

steps.keyText: Find his one hope, often a passed pawn, and stop it before anything else.

steps.setting: Your game against AgapelosLiberty, 16 Mar 2026. You are winning, but your king has few defenders. You played ((39.Qc6)).

moves.c: His only idea is checks against your king: after ((39.Qc6 Ra6 40.Qxa6 Qg4+)) his queen gives check after check. So hit his queen first.
Your queen blocks the check and offers a trade.
The queens are gone, and so are his checks. Your extra pawns now win.

steps.keyText: Checks against your king are his counterplay: trade his attacking queen before you go after more.

takefree.title: Take what is free, after a check for the catch
takefree.goal: Grab free material, but only after checking that it is really free.
takefree.rule: Free material makes the win easier, if nothing is hanging at home.
takefree.intro: More material makes winning easier, so do not be shy: if something is free, take it. But "free" needs one check. Is the piece really undefended? Does your capture leave something of yours hanging? And is there a bigger thing to take?

steps.setting: Your game against Zendop75, 1 Oct 2026. You played ((32.Rxa4)) after 5 seconds: the pawn looked free, but his bishop on c6 guards a4.

moves.c: The bishop is the real prize. If his pawn takes back, your other rook takes the queen on b8.
You have won a bishop.

steps.keyText: Before taking, check who guards the square, and look for the bigger capture.

steps.setting: Your game against Sergei-501, 22 Jan 2026. His queen on c7 is undefended. You played ((19...Qxc5+)) and took the knight with check instead.

moves.c: Take the biggest free thing. After ((19...Qxc5+ 20.Qxc5 bxc5 21.Bxa8)) you lose your rook too.
His bishop took your rook, but you have taken his queen and his knight.

steps.keyText: Count what each capture wins, and take the biggest one first.

allpieces.title: Bring everyone
allpieces.goal: Use all your pieces, and your king, before the final attack.
allpieces.rule: Before the final attack, the worst-placed piece joins; in the endgame that includes the king.
allpieces.intro: An attack with two pieces often runs out of steam; with three it usually wins. Before you start the final push, find your worst piece: the one doing nothing. Bring it closer first. In the endgame the king is a strong piece, so walk it towards the action.

steps.setting: Your game against traCys-Rarity, 14 Aug 2026. You are Black and your rook on b4 is doing nothing.

moves.c: Your second rook joins the attack on the pawn on f3. Two rooks against one defender.
You found this in the game: your pawn is now the only passed pawn on the board.

steps.keyText: Before you attack, ask which piece is doing nothing, and bring it in.

simplest.title: Choose the simplest win
simplest.goal: Prefer the safe, simple way to win.
simplest.rule: A clearly won endgame you know beats a flashy attack you have to calculate.
simplest.intro: When you are winning, you do not need the fastest win, only a safe one. Swapping into an endgame you know is often the best way. The Essential endgames course shows the ones to know: mate with queen or two rooks, the outside passed pawn, and the Lucena position.

steps.setting: Your game against Miky_il, 3 Nov 2026. You are a rook up.

moves.c: Swap off his last piece. You played this in the game.
Now he has no pieces left, and your rook and pawns win easily.

steps.keyText: When you are far ahead, swap off his last pieces and win the simple ending.

finish.title: Finish the job
finish.goal: Turn a big advantage into checkmate, and never give stalemate.
finish.rule: Far ahead: look for mate with checks, and never stalemate.
finish.intro: When you are far ahead, look at every check first: often there is a mate. And before every move, look at his king once more. If it has no move and he has no other move, it is stalemate, a draw. The Essential endgames lesson on stalemate shows the trap.

steps.setting: Your game against TRylo, 15 Dec 2025. You played ((56.Kd4)) in 2 seconds. His king had no move and his pawn was blocked: stalemate, a draw.

moves.c: Before you move, look at his king. Your queen move leaves him the square h3, so the game goes on.
Now your king can come closer: his king still has squares to go to.
Your king guards g1, and the queen gives mate.

steps.keyText: Before every move in a won ending, check that his king will still have a move.

courses.title: Essential endgames
courses.sub: The endings every club player must know, checked move by move against a database of perfect play.
courses.why: Many of your games are decided in the endgame, and most of them reach one of a handful of standard positions. Learn these and you stop throwing away won endings and stop losing drawn ones.

chapters.title: Basic checkmates
chapters.intro: A queen or a rook up is only a win if you can deliver mate. These four lessons give you a fixed method for each mate, and show the stalemate traps that turn a win into a draw.

chapters.title: King and pawn
chapters.intro: With only kings and pawns left, every single move counts. These lessons give you the counting tools: the square, key squares and the opposition. Everything later in the course is built on them.

chapters.title: More pawns
chapters.intro: With more pawns on the board, ideas decide the game, not only counting. An active king, a passed pawn far from the kings and a pawn majority win most pawn endings. These five lessons show how.

chapters.title: Queen and bishops
chapters.intro: A queen against a pawn about to queen, a bishop that cannot help its pawn, and bishops on opposite colours. In each one the material count lies: you must know which positions win and which are draws.

chapters.title: Rook endings
chapters.intro: Rook endings are the endings you will reach most often. A few rules decide most of them: rooks belong behind passed pawns, an active rook beats a passive one, and there are three positions every player must know by heart.

qmate.title: Queen checkmate
qmate.goal: Mate with king and queen against king, quickly and safely.
qmate.rule: Shrink his box with the queen a knight's move away, bring your king close, then mate on the edge.
qmate.intro: The queen alone cannot mate: your king must help. Use the queen to shrink the box the enemy king lives in, often from a knight's move away, so that he is never stalemated. When he is stuck on the edge, walk your king up and give mate. In the corner, look for the mate before anything else.

steps.setting: White to move. The black king is in the middle of the board.

moves.c: The queen cuts off the e-file: the king must stay on the left side.
Checks drive him towards the edge.
Now the king walks up to help.
A knight's move away from his king: it shrinks the box and leaves him a square.
Again a knight's move away.
Your king guards the queen and his king has nowhere to go.

steps.keyText: Queen a knight's move from his king, your king up close, then mate.

qstale.title: Don't stalemate him
qstale.goal: Finish a won ending without giving stalemate.
qstale.rule: Before every quiet move, check that his king still has a legal move.
qstale.intro: Stalemate means the side to move is not in check but has no legal move, and the game is a draw. It happens most when you are a queen up and play fast. Before each move that is not a check, ask one question: after this, can his king still move? If not, look for a check instead.

steps.setting: White to move. The natural ((1.Qg6)) is stalemate: the king on h8 cannot move and is not in check.

moves.c: This leaves the king the h7-square.
The queen is guarded by your king: mate.

steps.keyText: Leave his king one square until you can give mate.

rrmate.title: Two-rook ladder
rrmate.goal: Mate with two rooks without the help of your king.
rrmate.rule: One rook fences a line, the other checks on the next line; keep both far from his king.
rrmate.intro: Two rooks mate on their own, like climbing a ladder. One rook holds a rank, the other checks on the next rank, and they take turns. If his king comes close to a rook, move that rook far away along its line. Near the corner, watch out for stalemate.

steps.setting: White to move. Your king can stay at home.

moves.c: The first rook fences off the fifth rank.
The second rook checks on the next rank.
The rooks take turns, one rank higher each time.
The last rung of the ladder: mate on the back rank.

steps.keyText: Rooks take turns: one holds a rank, the other checks one rank further.

rmate.title: Rook checkmate
rmate.goal: Mate with king and rook against king.
rmate.rule: The rook cuts his king off; your king walks up to face his; then the rook checks him back a line.
rmate.intro: King and rook against king is a win, but only if your king helps. The rook builds a fence along a rank or file. Your king walks up until the two kings face each other with one square between. Then a rook check pushes him back one line. Keep the rook far from his king, or he just takes it.

steps.setting: White to move. The rook on the seventh rank keeps the black king on the back rank.

moves.c: The rook does the fencing, so your king walks up.
His king came close to the rook, so the rook moves far away along its rank.
Now the kings face each other on the b-file.
The rook checks along the back rank and the king has no square left.

steps.keyText: Fence with the rook, walk the king up to face his, then check along the edge.

square.title: The square rule
square.goal: Know at a glance whether a king can catch a passed pawn.
square.rule: Picture a square with the pawn's path as one side; if the king can step inside it, he catches the pawn.
square.intro: A passed pawn far from both kings starts a race. Counting moves one by one is slow and easy to get wrong in a 10-minute game. The square is a shortcut: the pawn's path to the last rank is one side of it. If the defending king can step into that square on his move, the pawn is caught. A pawn on its starting rank counts from one square further up, because it can jump two squares.

steps.setting: Black to move. The square of the c5-pawn has the corners c5, f5, f8 and c8.

moves.c: One diagonal step and the king is inside the square.
The square shrinks as the pawn moves, and the king stays inside it.
The pawn is caught and the game is a draw.

steps.keyText: Do not count moves: check whether the king can step into the square.

steps.setting: White to move. Right now the black king could still step into the square of the b4-pawn.

moves.c: Push at once. The new square runs from b5 to e8, and the king on g6 cannot reach it in one step.
The pawn queens: the king was one step too slow.

steps.keyText: When the king is just outside the square, push the pawn now before he steps in.

kpfront.title: King in front of the pawn
kpfront.goal: Win king and pawn against king by leading with your king.
kpfront.rule: Put your king two squares in front of the pawn, or next to that square, and the pawn will queen.
kpfront.intro: The three squares two steps in front of a pawn are its key squares: with your king on one, you win. So the king goes first and the pawn follows. Pushing the pawn too early is the classic way to turn a win into a draw.

steps.setting: White to move. The key squares of the d4-pawn are c6, d6 and e6.

moves.c: The king steps onto a key square. Now the pawn cannot be stopped.
The king clears the path. Black cannot get back in front of the pawn.
Only now does the pawn move, protected all the way.
The pawn has queened.

steps.keyText: King first, pawn second: walk the king to a key square, then push.

oppwin.title: The opposition: win
oppwin.goal: Use the {gl:opposition} to force your king through.
oppwin.rule: When the kings face each other with one square between, the side that must move has to give way.
oppwin.intro: This standoff is called the opposition: the kings face each other with one square between them, and whoever must move gives way. If you take the opposition, his king has to step aside and yours walks forward. When he steps aside, go round the other side: that is called outflanking.

steps.setting: Black to move. The kings face each other and Black has to give way.

moves.c: Black steps aside.
Go round the other side. Your king heads for the squares in front of the pawn.
Take the opposition again: now Black must give way once more.
A spare pawn move. The pawn stays back until the king has done its work.
The opposition once more, now on the fifth rank.
The king controls the queening square. The pawn walks through.

steps.keyText: Take the opposition, and when his king steps aside, go round the other side.

oppdraw.title: The opposition: hold
oppdraw.goal: Hold king and pawn against king as the defender.
oppdraw.rule: Stay in front of the pawn and face his king every time it steps forward.
oppdraw.intro: Now you are the defender. You hold the draw if you keep the opposition: the kings face each other with one square between, and he must move. When he steps up, step up to face him. When the pawn checks you, step straight back, never to the side.

steps.setting: White to move. Can White win? No: Black only has to face White's king.

moves.c: Face the king: Black keeps the opposition.
Face it again.
After the check, step straight back.
Straight back again, so you can face his king next move.
Stalemate: Black has no legal move, so it is a draw.

steps.keyText: Face his king when it steps forward, and step straight back after a pawn check.

kpdef.title: Get in front of the pawn
kpdef.goal: Defend king and pawn against king by blocking the pawn's path.
kpdef.rule: Run your king to the squares in front of the pawn; from there you can always face his king.
kpdef.intro: The defending king belongs on the pawn's path, in front of it. From there you can face the white king whenever it steps forward, and the pawn never gets through. A king beside or behind the pawn is usually too late.

steps.setting: Black to move. Your king is already in front of the pawn: keep it there.

moves.c: Stay on the pawn's path.
Face the king: one square between, and White must give way.
After the check, step back but stay in front of the pawn.
Face the king again.
The same pattern one rank higher. White makes no progress.

steps.keyText: Keep your king in front of the pawn and face his king whenever it steps up.

rookpawn.title: Rook pawn: run to the corner
rookpawn.goal: Draw against a rook pawn by reaching the corner in front of it.
rookpawn.rule: Against a rook pawn, get your king to the queening corner; nobody can push it out.
rookpawn.intro: A pawn on the a-file or h-file is special. Once the defending king reaches the corner in front of it, the attacker cannot push it out: every try ends in stalemate. So the defender runs for the corner, and the attacker must cut him off before he gets there.

steps.setting: Black to move. Your king is close to the h8 corner.

moves.c: Head for the corner.
Only this move: stay next to the corner.
Stalemate: Black has no legal move, so it is a draw.

steps.keyText: In the corner in front of a rook pawn you cannot be pushed out.

race.title: Pawn races
race.goal: Count a pawn race before you push, and stop his pawn first when you can.
race.rule: Count both pawns' moves to queen; if both would queen, stop his pawn with your king first.
race.intro: When both sides have a passed pawn, do not push on autopilot. Count how many moves each pawn needs to queen, and check whether each king can catch the other pawn with the square rule. If both pawns queen, it is usually a draw. Often the winning plan is quieter: your pawn runs on its own, and your king catches his.

steps.setting: White to move. Black's king cannot catch the a-pawn. Your king can still catch the f-pawn.

moves.c: Step into the square of the f-pawn first. If you push the a-pawn instead, Black's pawn queens as well.
The f-pawn is caught: if it moves, your king takes it.
Now push. Black's king is far too slow.
You have a queen and Black has nothing.

steps.keyText: If your pawn runs on its own, use the king to catch his pawn first.

activeking.title: The king is a fighting piece
activeking.goal: Use your king as an attacker as soon as the endgame starts.
activeking.rule: In the endgame, walk your king to the centre and into his half before you push pawns.
activeking.intro: In the middlegame the king hides. In the endgame there is little left to attack it, so it becomes a strong piece. A king in the centre can go to either side and eat pawns; a king on the edge only watches. When the queens come off, bring your king forward at once. With equal pawns, the side whose king arrives first usually wins.

steps.setting: White to move. The pawns are equal and mirror each other. Only the kings are different.

moves.c: Your king is closer to the centre: use that at once. Pawn moves can wait.
Head for the side his king has left.
Your king is deep in his half and his b-pawn is the target. His king has to defend, yours attacks: that difference wins the game.

steps.keyText: With equal pawns, the king that reaches the centre first decides the game.

outside.title: The outside passed pawn
outside.goal: Win a pawn ending with a passed pawn far from the kings.
outside.rule: Push the far passed pawn to pull his king away, then let your king eat his pawns on the other side.
outside.intro: A passed pawn has no enemy pawn in front of it or on the files next to it. When it is far from the kings, it works as a decoy, which means it pulls his king away from the real fight. Push it, and his king must run after it. While he is busy, your king walks to the other side and eats his pawns. You give up one pawn and win two.

steps.setting: White to move. Your a-pawn is passed and far from both kings.

moves.c: Push the far pawn: his king has to go after it.
Now your king goes the other way, to his pawns.
His king will take your a-pawn, but you have taken both his pawns. Your h-pawn queens long before his king can come back.

steps.keyText: Push the far pawn to drag his king away, then eat his pawns on the other side.

protpass.title: The protected passed pawn
protpass.goal: Win with a protected passed pawn: it ties his king down while yours attacks.
protpass.rule: A protected passed pawn ties his king down; leave it where it is and attack with your king.
protpass.intro: A protected passed pawn is a passed pawn guarded by one of your pawns. His king cannot take it, but must stay near it to stop it. So his king is tied down and yours is free. Do not rush the pawn forward: once it leaves the protection of your other pawn, his king takes it. Walk your king to his other pawns instead and eat them.

steps.setting: White to move. Your d5 pawn is passed and protected by the c4 pawn.

moves.c: Your king goes up the board towards his h-pawn.
His king cannot take d5, because the c4 pawn protects it.
You are a pawn up, and his king still has to watch your d-pawn. The rest is a matter of time.

steps.keyText: Leave the protected pawn where it is and use your free king to eat his pawns.

majority.title: Make a passed pawn from a majority
majority.goal: Turn a pawn majority into a passed pawn.
majority.rule: With more pawns on one side, push first the pawn that has no enemy pawn in front of it.
majority.intro: A majority means you have more pawns than he has on one side of the board. A majority can make a passed pawn, but the order matters. Push first the pawn with no enemy pawn in front of it; it is called the candidate. The other pawns follow and support it. Push the wrong pawn first and you waste a move, or your pawns get stuck.

steps.setting: White to move. You have two pawns against one on the queenside. Which one goes first?

moves.c: The b-pawn has no enemy pawn in front of it, so it goes first.
Now your a-pawn is passed, and his king is too far away to catch it.
Stop his b-pawn first.
The majority has made a new queen.

steps.keyText: Push the pawn with no enemy pawn in front of it first, and a passed pawn appears.

breakthru.title: Pawn breakthrough
breakthru.goal: Break through with three pawns against three when his king is far away.
breakthru.rule: Push the middle pawn; when he captures, push the pawn on the other side, and one pawn queens.
breakthru.intro: Three pawns facing three pawns look blocked. But when his king is far away, you can give up two pawns to make the third a queen. Push the middle pawn first. Whatever he takes with, push the pawn on the other side, and he cannot stop both. Count first: it only works when his king cannot catch the last pawn. If he is to move, he stops it by pushing his own middle pawn.

steps.setting: White to move. Both kings are far away on the queenside.

moves.c: The middle pawn goes first. If he ignores it, it takes on f7 or h7 and queens.
Push the pawn on the other side of his capture. After ((2...gxh5 3.fxg7)) the g-pawn queens.
Nothing can stop the h-pawn now: his king is five files away.

steps.keyText: Middle pawn first, then the pawn on the other side of his capture: one of them queens.

qvp.title: Queen against a pawn on the 7th
qvp.goal: Beat a centre or knight pawn on the seventh rank with your queen.
qvp.rule: Force his king in front of the pawn with checks, then use the free move to bring your king closer.
qvp.intro: A pawn one step from queening, with its king beside it, looks dangerous. Against a centre pawn or a knight pawn the queen still wins. Check and attack the pawn until his king has to step in front of it. While it stands there, the pawn cannot move, so you have one free move to bring your king one step closer. Repeat until your king arrives.

steps.setting: White to move. Your king is far away on h8.

moves.c: Pin the pawn: it cannot queen while the queen watches d1.
His king now stands in front of the pawn.
The free move: your king steps closer.
In front of the pawn again.
Another free move. Your king keeps coming until it can help.

steps.keyText: Each time his king blocks his own pawn, your king takes one step closer.

qvpdraw.title: …and when it is a draw
qvpdraw.goal: Know when a queen cannot beat a pawn on the seventh, and hold it as the defender.
qvpdraw.rule: A rook pawn or bishop pawn on the seventh, its king beside it and the enemy king far away, is a draw.
qvpdraw.intro: The method of the last lesson fails against a pawn on the a-, c-, f- or h-file. With a rook pawn the defender goes into the corner and is stalemated. With a bishop pawn he goes to the corner too: if the queen takes the pawn, it is stalemate. So as the defender, head for the corner; as the attacker, know it is a draw unless your king is close.

steps.setting: White to move. Can White win? No: the bishop pawn saves Black.

wrongb.title: The wrong bishop
wrongb.goal: Spot the draw with a rook pawn and the wrong bishop.
wrongb.rule: A rook pawn plus a bishop that cannot cover the queening square is a draw once the defender's king reaches the corner.
wrongb.intro: Say the rook pawn queens on a dark square and the bishop runs on light squares. Then the bishop can never drive the king out of the corner. So the defender runs for the corner and stays there. The attacker must keep his king out of the corner, or the win is gone.

moves.c: Head for the corner.
Into the corner.

ocb.title: Opposite-coloured bishops
ocb.goal: Hold an ending with bishops of opposite colours, even pawns down.
ocb.rule: Blockade the pawns on the colour his bishop cannot touch, and let your bishop guard the squares in front of them.
ocb.intro: When the bishops run on different colours, the defender often draws even two pawns down. His bishop can never chase your king off a square of your bishop's colour, and your bishop guards the squares his pawns need. Put your king in front of the pawns and keep the bishop on a long diagonal. Pawns that cannot move forward cannot win.

Stay close to the pawns.

steps.keyText: King in front of the pawns, bishop on the squares they need: two pawns down is still a draw.

rbehind.title: Rooks belong behind passed pawns
rbehind.goal: Put your rook behind a passed pawn, whether it is yours or his.
rbehind.rule: Put the rook behind the passed pawn: behind yours it pushes, behind his it gains room as the pawn moves.
rbehind.intro: A rook behind its own passed pawn supports it all the way, and the further the pawn runs, the more room the rook has. A rook in front of the pawn is stuck there. The same holds in defence: your rook behind his passed pawn keeps attacking it from behind.

steps.setting: Black to move. White has a passed a-pawn. Where does your rook belong?

moves.c: Behind the pawn: from a2 it attacks the pawn on every square it moves to.
White's king came too late, and the pawn falls.

steps.keyText: Against a passed pawn, put your rook behind it.

r7th.title: The active rook
r7th.goal: Use your rook actively: attack pawns and take the seventh rank.
r7th.rule: Put your rook where it attacks, on the seventh rank or behind his pawns, and make his rook the one that defends.
r7th.intro: A rook that attacks pawns or stands on the seventh rank ties his whole army down. A rook that only guards pawns is a bad piece. In rook endings ask: where does my rook attack something? That square is usually the right one, even if it costs a pawn.

cutoff.title: Cut the king off
cutoff.goal: Win rook and pawn against rook by keeping his king away from your pawn.
cutoff.rule: Put your rook on the file between his king and your pawn, then bring your king up before the pawn.
cutoff.intro: In rook endings the defender's king is his best defender. If your rook stands on a file between his king and your pawn, his king is cut off: it cannot cross that file. With his king cut off by two files or more, rook and pawn against rook is usually a win. Keep the fence, walk your king in front of the pawn, and push the pawn behind it.

The rook comes back behind the pawn, still on the near side.

lucena.title: Lucena: build a bridge
lucena.goal: Win the most important rook ending: pawn on the seventh, your king in front of it.
lucena.rule: Check his king away, put your rook on the fourth rank, walk your king out, and block the checks with the rook.
lucena.intro: This is the winning position every rook ending aims for. Your king sits in front of the pawn on the seventh, and his rook keeps checking. The plan: drive his king one more file away with a check and lift your rook to the fourth rank. Then walk your king out and block the checks with the rook. That block is called building a bridge.

moves.c: First push his king one more file away.
The bridge: the rook goes to the fourth rank.
The rook blocks the check: the bridge is built and the pawn queens.

philidor.title: Philidor: third-rank defence
philidor.goal: Hold rook and pawn against rook with the Philidor defence.
philidor.rule: King in front of the pawn, rook on your third rank; when the pawn steps onto it, check from behind.
philidor.intro: This is the most important drawing method in rook endings. Your king stands in front of the pawn, and your rook guards your third rank, so his king cannot come forward. When the pawn steps onto that rank, his king loses its shelter: your rook drops to the back and checks from behind. The checks never end.

The pawn steps onto the sixth rank, so White's king has no shelter in front of it any more.
Now the rook goes to the back and checks from behind.
The checks go on forever: a draw.

longside.title: Check from far away
longside.goal: Hold rook and pawn against rook when Philidor is too late.
longside.rule: King to the short side of the pawn, rook to the long side, and check from far away.
longside.intro: If his king already stands on your third rank, the Philidor defence is too late. Then your king goes to the short side of the pawn, the side with fewer files to the edge. Your rook goes to the long side and checks from a distance. Checks from close by run out; from far away they never do.

also.d8e7: Also in front of the pawn; both hold.

wrong.d8d7: Your king is on the wrong side and White's rook takes your third rank.

philidor-1.why: First the king: it must stand in front of the pawn. Only then does the rook defence work.

also.e8d7: Also in front of the pawn; both hold.

wrong.e8e7: His rook takes your third rank and his king walks in.

philidor-2.why: Put your king in front of the c-pawn's path before anything else.

also.c8d7: Also stands in front of the pawn; both hold.

wrong.c8c7: Your king is too far from the pawn's path and his rook cuts you off.

philidor-3.why: The defending king belongs on the pawn's file, in front of it.

also.f8e7: Also blocks the pawn's path; both hold.

wrong.f8f7: His rook takes the sixth rank and your king is shut out.

philidor-4.why: Same rule: king in front of the pawn first, then the third-rank rook.

wrong.a4a5: The checks run out and White's king shelters in front of the pawn.

longside-1.why: Put your king on the short side, in front of the pawn. Your rook stays on the long side, far away.

wrong.f7g8: Your king is too far from the pawn and it marches on.

longside-2.why: Your king goes in front of the pawn's path. Wandering off to the side lets the pawn run.

wrong.f8g8: Your king walked away from the pawn and White wins.

longside-3.why: Step in front of the pawn. From e8 your king blocks d7 and d8 together with your rook's checks.

qmate-p.text: You are White. Shrink the box, bring your king, and mate without stalemate.

qstale-p.text: You are White. Mate the king in the corner, and check every quiet move for stalemate.

rrmate-p.text: You are White. Climb the ladder with the rooks and keep them away from his king.

rmate-p.text: You are White. Fence him in with the rook, bring your king, and mate on the edge.

square-p.text: You are Black. Catch the b-pawn: find the one move that steps into its square.

square-p2.text: You are White. Check the square before you move, then queen the pawn.

kpfront-p.text: You are White. King first, pawn second: queen the pawn.

oppwin-p.text: You are White and Black moves first. Take the opposition, go round, then queen.

oppdraw-p.text: You are Black. Stay in front of the pawn and face White's king every time.

kpdef-p.text: You are Black. Get in front of the pawn and stay there.

rookpawn-p.text: You are Black. Run for the corner before White's king shuts you out.

race-p.text: You are White. Count the race first: whose pawn queens, and can your king catch his?

activeking-p.text: You are Black. His king is far from the centre: march yours to the centre and into his half, then go after his pawns.

outside-p.text: You are White, a pawn up. Push the a-pawn to drag his king away, then eat his kingside pawns.

protpass-p.text: You are White. Your d-pawn ties his king down: use your king to win his other pawns.

majority-p.text: You are White. Make a passed pawn with the right pawn first, and do not forget his h-pawn.

breakthru-p.text: You are White. Push the middle pawn, then the pawn on the other side of his capture.

qvp-p.text: You are White. Stop the pawn, force his king in front of it, bring your king and mate.

qvpdraw-p.text: You are Black. Keep your king next to the pawn and use the corner.

wrongb-p.text: You are Black. Stay in the corner and let White find no way through.

ocb-p.text: You are Black, two pawns down. Blockade the pawns and keep your bishop on the dark squares.

rbehind-p.text: You are White. Put your rook behind the pawn and push it home.

r7th-p.text: You are White. Put your rook on the seventh rank and go after the pawn on c7. Then bring your king and pawns forward.

cutoff-p.text: You are White. Keep his king cut off, bring your king up, then push.

lucena-p.text: You are White. Check, bridge on the fourth rank, walk out, block.

philidor-p.text: You are Black. Rook on the sixth rank until the pawn arrives, then check from behind.

longside-p.text: You are Black. Keep your king on the short side and check from far away.

courses.title: Tactics ABC
courses.sub: The patterns behind most won and lost pieces: learn the clue, watch it work, then practise until you see it at a glance.
courses.why: In your 175 analysed games you left a piece hanging 49 times, missed a free capture 33 times and ran into a fork 35 times. These are short tactics, one or two moves deep. Each lesson teaches one pattern and, above all, the clue on the board that tells you it is there.

chapters.title: Free pieces
chapters.intro: A free piece is one that nobody defends. Taking one costs you nothing, and losing one costs you the game. This chapter trains one habit: after every move, look for pieces that nothing defends, his and yours.

chapters.title: Count before you capture
chapters.intro: When a piece is defended, taking it starts a string of captures on one square. Count the attackers and the defenders before you start, and you know who comes out ahead.

chapters.title: Checkmate in one
chapters.intro: Most mates in real games use one of a few patterns. Learn to recognise them, and look at every check before any other move.

chapters.title: The back rank
chapters.intro: A king behind a wall of its own pawns is safe from the front but helpless from behind. Use this against him, and make sure he cannot use it against you.

chapters.title: Forks
chapters.intro: A fork is one move that attacks two things at once. He can save only one of them. Knights are the best forkers, but every piece can do it, even a pawn.

chapters.title: Pins
chapters.intro: A pinned piece stands in front of something bigger on the same line. If it moves, the bigger piece is lost, or, when the king stands behind it, it cannot move at all.

chapters.title: Skewers
chapters.intro: A skewer is a pin turned around: the big piece stands in front. You attack it, it must move, and you take the piece behind.

chapters.title: Discovered attacks and double check
chapters.intro: When one of your pieces stands in front of another on a line, moving the front piece uncovers an attack. If the piece that moves makes a threat of its own, he faces two threats at once.

chapters.title: Remove the defender
chapters.intro: Every defender has a job. Take it, trade it or chase it away, and the piece it was guarding is left alone.

chapters.title: Lure and drag away
chapters.intro: A defender can be dragged away from its post, and a king can be lured onto a bad square. Both work because a piece can only be in one place at a time.

chapters.title: Trapped pieces
chapters.intro: A piece that has gone too far, or stands in a corner, may have no safe square at all. Attack it, and it is lost.

chapters.title: In-between moves
chapters.intro: When he takes one of your pieces, taking back is not compulsory. First look for a check or a bigger threat; the recapture can usually wait one move.

chapters.title: Mate in two
chapters.intro: A mate in two is a check, a forced reply, and a mate. Many of them start with a sacrifice, so you must picture the position after his only answer.

chapters.title: Find the defence
chapters.intro: Tactics are not only for attacking. When he threatens something real, there is often exactly one move that holds. Find it by naming his threat first.

chapters.title: Pawn tricks
chapters.intro: A pawn that is about to become a queen changes everything. Pieces get sacrificed to stop it, and to push it through.

chapters.title: Course exam
chapters.intro: No new patterns here. The positions are mixed, so you do not know in advance which tactic is coming, just as in a real game.

loose.title: Free pieces
loose.goal: Spot a piece nobody defends, yours or his.
loose.rule: After every move, ask: which pieces are undefended now, his and mine?
loose.intro: In your games you left a piece hanging 49 times. Another 33 times you did not take a piece he left for you. Both mistakes have the same cure. After each move, his or yours, scan the board for pieces that nothing defends. It takes a few seconds, and it is the most valuable habit in chess.

steps.setting: Black's rook has just given check on d1. Your queen and his queen face each other.

moves.c: The rook gives check, but no black piece defends it. Take it with the king.
The queens come off the board.
He picked up a pawn, but you are a whole rook ahead.

steps.keyText: When a piece gives check, first ask who defends it: a checking piece with no defender is just a free piece.

steps.setting: Your game against Caro-6, 3 Mar 2026. Black has just pushed a pawn to a5.

moves.c: His knight on b6 was defended by a pawn on a7. That pawn has moved to a5, so the knight is now free. You took it.
Your queen steps back with a whole extra knight.

steps.keyText: When a pawn moves forward, look at what it was defending: that piece may now be free.

steps.setting: Your game against laleta34, 18 May 2026. Black's bishop has just gone to b3. You played ((29.Nb7)) here.

moves.c: The bishop on b3 is attacked by your pawn and nothing defends it. Take it. In the game you moved the knight, and after ((29.Nb7 Rxa4)) your extra piece was gone.
You are a bishop up.

steps.keyText: Before any plan of your own, check whether his last move left something you can take for free.

count.title: Count before you capture
count.goal: Work out who wins a string of captures on one square.
count.rule: Count attackers and defenders; start with the cheapest piece, and remember that a trade can remove a defender.
count.intro: Thirty-four of your mistakes lost material in a trade. A piece with more attackers than defenders can be won, but only if you capture in the right order: cheapest piece first. And a defender is not always a real defender: if it can be traded off, or cannot take back safely, do not count it.

steps.setting: White to move. Count the pieces aiming at the pawn on d5.

moves.c: Two attackers (knight and rook) against one defender (the knight on f6). Start with the cheaper piece, the knight. Starting with the rook would be wrong: after ((1.Rxd5 Nxd5 2.Nxd5)) you have given a rook for a knight and a pawn.
The last capture is yours, and you are a pawn up.

steps.keyText: More attackers than defenders wins the target, as long as you capture with the cheapest piece first.

steps.setting: Black's bishop has just come to f5. Your bishop attacks it, and his queen defends it.

moves.c: One attacker, one defender: taking the bishop now only trades it, as in ((15.Bxf5 Qxf5)). So first trade off the defender.
Now nothing defends the bishop on f5, and you have won it.

steps.keyText: When the count is level, look for a trade that takes away one of the defenders.

steps.setting: Your game against Baterdene_Bachka, 25 Mar 2026. Your knight on d4 is attacked by a pawn. You played ((22...Nf5)) here.

moves.c: Retreat the knight to a safe square. On f5 it looks defended by the pawn on e6, but that pawn cannot take back: after ((22...Nf5 23.Qxf5 exf5 24.Rxe7)) your queen falls. So on f5 your knight would have no real defender.
Your knight is safe and the material is level.

steps.keyText: A defender that cannot take back without losing something bigger does not count.

mate1.title: Checkmate patterns in one
mate1.goal: Recognise the everyday mates: queen next to the king, two rooks, the knight in the corner, and pieces working together.
mate1.rule: Look at every check first: for each one, count the squares his king can still reach.
mate1.intro: A mate needs three things: a check, no square for the king, and no way to take or block the checking piece. The quickest way to find one is a fixed habit. Before any other move, look at every check you have. For each check, ask where his king can go. If the answer is nowhere, it is mate.

steps.setting: White to move. His king on h8 is boxed in by his own knight and pawn.

moves.c: Check along the h-file. The king cannot go to g8 or g7, because his own pieces stand there, and h7 is covered by your queen. Nothing can block or take her: mate.

steps.keyText: A king boxed in by its own pieces needs only one check on an open line.

steps.setting: Your game against toehats, 2 Feb 2026. His king has just stepped into the corner.

moves.c: You found it. The rook checks on the h-file, and your other rook on g1 controls the whole g-file, so the king has no square. Two rooks side by side, one checking and one guarding, give mate.

steps.keyText: Two rooks mate together: one gives check, the other takes away the next line.

steps.setting: Your game against albert_sebastian, 20 Feb 2026. Black has just pushed a pawn on the queenside.

moves.c: You found this one too. The pawn on g7 cannot take back, because your rook on c7 pins it to the king. The rook on g6 is guarded by your pawn on f5, so the king has nowhere to go.

steps.keyText: Check every capture next to his king: a pinned pawn is not a real defender.

backrank.title: The back rank
backrank.goal: Use, and avoid, the king stuck behind its own pawns.
backrank.rule: If his king has no escape square, every rook or queen check on the back rank is a threat.
backrank.intro: Look at the king and the three pawns in front of it. If none of them has moved, the king has no escape square. Then a rook or queen landing on the back rank with check is mate, unless something can block or take it. Eleven of your mistakes allowed a mate. Count who guards the back rank, for both kings.

steps.setting: Black to move. Look at the white king on h1 and the pawns in front of it.

moves.c: His king has no escape square: his own pawns on g2 and h2 take the squares in front of it. Your rook takes on f1 with check, your queen covers g1, and nothing can block or take your rook.

steps.keyText: A king behind unmoved pawns is mated by any safe check along the back rank.

steps.setting: Your game against matteoperugia, 23 Dec 2025. His rook has just come to e4. You played ((29...Nd5)) here.

moves.c: Nothing defends his rook on e4, so take it. In the game you moved the knight, and after ((29...Nd5 30.Rxe8+ Rxe8 31.Qxe8#)) your king was caught on the back rank. Your king on h8 has no air, so the rook on e8 must stay defended.
You have won a rook, and your back rank is safe again.

steps.keyText: When your king has no escape square, check twice before moving a piece that guards the back rank.

steps.setting: Your game against hazemalassaf, 26 Mar 2026. His rook on d1 controls the open d-file. You played ((19...Rf7)) here.

moves.c: His rook threatens to check on d8. Your king could step to h7, but his knight on g6 covers h8, so a rook check there would be mate. Your rook goes to e8 and guards the back rank. In the game, after ((19...Rf7 20.Rd8+ Rf8 21.Rxf8+ Kh7 22.Rh8#)) it was over.
Your back rank is covered, and you can think about your own plans again.

steps.keyText: If his rook or queen can reach your back rank with check, guard that rank first or make an escape square.

fork-knight.title: Knight forks
fork-knight.rule: Look for two valuable pieces a knight's jump apart, and a safe square that hits both.
fork-knight.intro: A knight attacks in a strange shape, so people forget about it. That is why forks cost you 35 mistakes in your games. The clue is simple: find two of his valuable pieces, the king, queen or rooks, that a knight on one square would attack together. Then check that the square is safe, or that the move comes with check.

steps.setting: White to move. Look at his king on e6 and his rook on h3.

moves.c: The knight checks the king and attacks the rook at the same time.
The king had to move, and you take the rook.

steps.keyText: A knight check that also hits a rook or queen wins it, because the check must be answered first.

steps.setting: Your game against ant-lop8, 16 Aug 2026. His bishop has just come to e6.

moves.c: You found it. The knight takes a pawn with check and attacks the rook on a8. If his queen takes the knight, your bishop on f4 takes the queen.
You won his queen for a knight.

steps.keyText: A knight check next to his king often hits a rook in the corner as well.

steps.setting: Your game against AintGenius, 23 Mar 2026. He has just pushed a pawn to a3 to chase your knight.

moves.c: You found it again. The knight checks the king and attacks the rook on a1 from the same square.
You won a whole rook.

steps.keyText: When he chases your knight, look at every square it can jump to: one of them may be a fork.

fork-other.title: Pawn, queen and rook forks
fork-other.goal: Every piece can fork: pawns, queens, rooks and bishops.
fork-other.rule: Look for two of his pieces on one line or diagonal, or side by side in front of your pawn.
fork-other.intro: A pawn fork is the cheapest win in chess: the pawn is worth less than either piece it attacks. A queen fork often comes with check, so he has no time to save the second piece. The clue is two of his pieces that one of your pieces could hit from a single square. Look especially at loose pieces and at his king.

steps.setting: Black to move. His two rooks stand side by side on d3 and f3.

moves.c: Your pawn attacks both rooks at once. He can save only one.
The pawn takes the other rook.
He took the pawn, but you have won a rook for it.

steps.keyText: Two pieces side by side, one square in front of your pawn: push the pawn between them.

steps.setting: White to move. His bishop on h6 and his king on h8 are on the same file.

moves.c: The rook takes a pawn with check and attacks the bishop on h6 along the file.
The king had to move, and the bishop falls.

steps.keyText: A check along a file or rank that also attacks a loose piece behind is a fork.

steps.setting: Your game against benjonas27, 16 Jan 2026. He has just taken a pawn on d5 with his knight. You played ((16.Qc2)) here.

moves.c: The queen takes a knight with check and also attacks the rook on a8. In the game you moved the queen away, and after ((16.Qc2 Ndb4)) his knight attacked your queen and bishop.
You have won a knight and a rook.

steps.keyText: A queen capture with check gives you a second move: use it to take the next loose piece.

pin.title: Pins
pin.goal: Use a piece that cannot move because something bigger stands behind it.
pin.rule: A pinned piece does not really defend anything: attack it again, or take what it is supposed to guard.
pin.intro: Look along every line from your bishops, rooks and queen. When two of his pieces stand on that line with the bigger one behind, you have a pin. Pinned to the king, the piece cannot move at all. Pinned to the queen, it can move, but he loses the queen. Then pile up on the pinned piece: it cannot run away.

steps.setting: White to move. Your bishop on b5 pins his knight on c6 to his king on e8.

moves.c: The pawn attacks the knight. The knight cannot move, because that would expose his king to your bishop.
He saved the king from the pin, but the knight was lost: you won a piece for a pawn.

steps.keyText: A pinned piece cannot run away: attack it with something cheap, ideally a pawn.

steps.setting: Black to move. His queen on d2 and his king on c1 stand on one diagonal.

moves.c: Your bishop attacks the queen, and the king behind her pins her. She cannot step away, so he gives her up for the bishop.
You have won his queen for a bishop.

steps.keyText: Look along the diagonals from his king: a queen standing on one can be pinned by a bishop.

steps.setting: White to move. Your bishop on b3 pins his rook on f7 to his king on g8.

moves.c: A queen check on the back rank. His rook on f7 cannot block on f8, because it is pinned.
His other rook took the queen, and your rook mates on the back rank.

steps.keyText: A pinned piece cannot help its king: count it out when you look for mate.

skewer.title: Skewers
skewer.goal: Attack the big piece and win the one behind it when it moves.
skewer.rule: When his king or queen stands in front of another piece on one line, check or attack along that line.
skewer.intro: The most common skewer is a check. His king stands on a line, and further along the same line stands a rook or queen. You give check along that line, the king must step aside, and you take what was hiding behind it. Look for it whenever his king is out in the open, especially in the endgame.

steps.setting: White to move. His king on d4 and his queen on d1 stand on the same file.

moves.c: Check along the d-file. The king must step off the file, and then your rook takes the queen behind it.
A whole queen for nothing.

steps.keyText: King and queen on one file, rank or diagonal: check along that line and take the queen.

steps.setting: White to move. His king on e7 and his queen on d8 stand on one diagonal.

moves.c: The bishop checks along the diagonal g5-d8. Behind the king stands his queen.
The king had to move, and the queen falls.

steps.keyText: A bishop check can skewer too: look along the diagonals through his king.

steps.setting: Black to move. His king on e1 and his rook on g1 stand on the first rank.

moves.c: Check along the first rank. When the king steps off it, the rook on g1 behind it is yours.
You have won a whole rook.

steps.keyText: In the endgame, look along the ranks too: king and rook side by side are a skewer waiting to happen.

discovered.title: Discovered attacks and double check
discovered.goal: Move one piece and uncover the attack of another.
discovered.rule: The piece that moves away can go anywhere with a threat of its own: a check, a capture, or an attack.
discovered.intro: Look for your bishop, rook or queen hidden behind one of your own pieces, aiming at something of his. Now move the front piece with a threat: a check is best. He must answer that threat, and the uncovered attack wins. When both pieces give check, it is a double check: the king must move, because nothing can block two checks at once.

steps.setting: White to move. Your pawn on d3 stands between your bishop and his rook on b1.

moves.c: The pawn gives check, and by moving it uncovers your bishop's attack on the rook.
The king had to deal with the check, and the rook falls.
You are a whole bishop up.

steps.keyText: Even a pawn can uncover an attack: move it with check and the piece behind does the rest.

steps.setting: White to move. Your knight on g5 stands between your queen and his king.

moves.c: Double check: the knight checks the king, and your queen behind it checks along the g-file. Nothing can block both, so the king must move.
The queen comes to g7, guarded by the knight, and it is mate.

steps.keyText: Against a double check the king must move: look where it can go before anything else.

steps.setting: White to move. Your knight on f3 stands between your rook on f2 and his bishop on f5.

moves.c: The knight takes his knight, and at the same moment your rook attacks the bishop on f5.
He took back the knight, and your rook takes the bishop. You have won a piece.

steps.keyText: A capture by the front piece is the strongest way to uncover an attack: he cannot answer both.

removal.title: Remove the defender
removal.goal: Take or chase away the piece that guards the target.
removal.rule: Ask what job the defending piece has, then take it, trade it or chase it away.
removal.intro: When the piece you want is defended, do not give up. Look at its defender instead. Can you take the defender, trade it off, or force it to move? Often you can even capture the defender with check or with a threat, so he has no time to rescue anything. Then the target is free.

steps.setting: White to move. Your rook attacks his knight on b6. What guards it?

moves.c: The knight on b6 is guarded only by the pawn on c7. Take his queen: he must take back with that pawn.
The pawn left c7, the knight lost its only defender, and your rook takes it.

steps.keyText: If a pawn is the only defender, force it to capture something else.

steps.setting: White to move. His knight on f2 attacks your rooks, and his bishop on d4 guards it.

moves.c: Take the defender.
His bishop is gone, so nothing guards the knight, and your rook takes it.

steps.keyText: When his piece attacks you from a defended square, take the defender first.

steps.setting: White to move. Your rook attacks his bishop on e5, and his knight on g6 guards it.

moves.c: Take the defender.
Now nothing guards the bishop, and your rook takes it.

steps.keyText: When the defender can be taken, take it first and collect the target afterwards.

deflect.title: Lure and drag away
deflect.goal: Force a defender to leave its post, or drag a king onto a bad square.
deflect.rule: A piece with two jobs can do only one: give it a reason to leave.
deflect.intro: Find a piece of his that does an important job: guarding a square, a piece or his back rank. Now attack it, check it, or offer it something it must take. When it leaves, the job is undone. This is called a {gl:deflection}. Luring his king onto a square where it can be attacked works the same way.

steps.setting: Black to move. His rook on d6 is guarded only by his king on c5.

moves.c: Give up your rook to drag the king away from d6.
His king took your rook, but now his rook has no guard and your king takes it. You are left with a pawn ending, a pawn up.

steps.keyText: When a single piece guards something, see if you can force that piece to take something else.

steps.setting: White to move. His king on h5 has very few squares.

moves.c: The pawn checks, and the king cannot take it because your pawn on h3 guards g4. It must step to h4.
On h4 the king is boxed in by your pawns, and the rook takes on h6 with mate.

steps.keyText: A check can drive his king onto a square where your next move is mate.

steps.setting: White to move. His pawn on h5 is guarded only by his king on h4.

moves.c: Check with the pawn. The king cannot take it, because your rook on g7 guards g3, so it must step to h3.
The king has been dragged away from h5, and your rook takes the pawn with mate.

steps.keyText: Drag the king away with a check, then take what it was guarding.

trapped.title: Trapped pieces
trapped.goal: Win a piece that has no safe square.
trapped.rule: Before you grab a pawn deep in his camp, ask: how does my piece get out?
trapped.intro: When one of his pieces goes deep into your half, count its squares. If every square it could go to is guarded, one attack wins it. Pawns are the best trappers, because nothing is cheaper. And when you are the one grabbing a pawn with your queen, count her way back first.

steps.setting: White to move. Look at his bishop on h5 and the squares around it.

moves.c: The pawn attacks the bishop. It cannot retreat to g6 or towards e8, because his own king is in the way. The other diagonal is blocked by your pawn.
He had to give the bishop for a pawn.

steps.keyText: A bishop on the edge with its own pieces in the way has very few squares: one pawn can trap it.

steps.setting: Black to move. His queen has just taken a pawn on g7.

moves.c: The bishop attacks the queen. Every square she could go to is guarded, so she cannot escape.
He gets a rook for his queen, and you are well ahead.

steps.keyText: A queen that grabs a pawn next to your king can often be trapped there.

steps.setting: Black to move. His rook on a1 is stuck in the corner behind his knight.

moves.c: Take the pawn: now your queen attacks the rook on a1, which has no safe square.
The rook was trapped in its corner, and your queen takes it.

steps.keyText: Rooks and knights still at home can be trapped: look at them when his pawn in front of them falls.

between.title: In-between moves
between.goal: Before the obvious recapture, look for a check or a bigger threat.
between.rule: You do not have to recapture at once: first look for a check or a capture of something bigger.
between.intro: After a capture your hand moves by itself to take back. Stop for a moment. Is there a check, or a capture of a bigger piece, that he must answer first? Play that, and take back afterwards. This is called an in-between move ({gl:intermezzo}). It often wins a whole piece, because his piece is still hanging when you come back to it.

steps.setting: White to move. His knight has just taken on c1, and his bishop on c4 attacks your bishop on e2.

moves.c: Take his bishop first, with check. Taking the knight at once with ((31.Nxc1)) leaves your bishop attacked, and you lose a piece back.
Now take back the knight. You have won a whole bishop.

steps.keyText: When two of your pieces are attacked, look for a capture with check: it saves one and wins time for the other.

steps.setting: Black to move. His queen has just taken a pawn on d5, offering a queen trade.

moves.c: Before taking the queen, take his knight with check. If you take the queen first, ((8...Qxd5 9.Nxd5)) his knight takes back.
Now the knight is gone, nothing takes back on d5, and you have won his queen.

steps.keyText: Before you trade, take the piece that would take back, if you can do it with check.

steps.setting: White to move. His bishop has just taken your pawn on g4, and your rook on f4 attacks it. Look at his rook on e8 too.

moves.c: Before taking the bishop, take his rook with check.

mate2.title: Mate in two
mate2.goal: Check, forced reply, mate: rook ladders, smothered mates and queen sacrifices on the back rank.
mate2.rule: Checks first; for each check, picture the position after his only reply and look for mate there.
mate2.intro: When his king has few squares, try every check, even the ones that give up a piece. For each one, ask: what can he do? If he has only one answer, picture the board after it and look for a mate. Three patterns come up again and again. Two rooks take turns to check. A knight mates a king boxed in by its own pieces. A sacrifice clears the back rank.

steps.setting: White to move. His king on g8 has few squares, and your pawn on g6 guards f7.

moves.c: The queen checks from f7, guarded by the pawn on g6. The king has only one square.
Now the queen takes the knight with check. The king cannot go to h7 because of your pawn, and it is mate.

steps.keyText: A pawn deep in his camp can guard your queen right next to his king.

steps.setting: White to move. His king on h8 is surrounded by its own pieces.

moves.c: Take his rook with check. His only answer is to block on g8 with the knight.
Smothered mate: the king is surrounded by its own pieces, and the knight check cannot be blocked.

steps.keyText: A king in the corner, boxed in by its own pieces, can be mated by a single knight check.

steps.setting: Your game against easyyyy04, 10 Nov 2026. He has just taken your piece on e7, and his king on g1 has no escape square.

The rook takes the knight, and his own pawns trap his king. Mate in two.

defend.title: Find the defence
defend.goal: He threatens something real: find the move that holds.
defend.rule: First name his threat, then choose: take, block, move away, or counter-attack with something bigger.
defend.intro: Fifty of your mistakes were answered by a check. Most of them came when you were busy with your own plans. When he makes a threat, put it into words first: "he wants to check on e8", "he wants to take my rook". Then look at your four ways out: take the attacker, block the line, move away, or make a bigger threat. Pick the one that leaves nothing loose.

steps.setting: White to move. His rook checks your king.

moves.c: You must answer the check, so pick the answer that does the most. On e6 your king attacks both of his rooks at once.
He saved one rook by taking your pawn, and you took the other.

steps.keyText: When you must move your king out of check, look for the square where it also attacks something.

promote.title: Pawn tricks
promote.goal: Push a pawn through with a sacrifice or a check that gains time.
promote.rule: A pawn two steps from queening is worth a piece: count how many moves it needs and who can stop it.
promote.intro: When a pawn is close to the last rank, normal values no longer count. A rook can be given up to clear its path, and a check can win the one move you need. Ask three questions. What stops my pawn? Can I remove or distract that piece? Can I move with check, so that he has no time?

steps.setting: Black to move. Your pawn on c2 is one step from queening.

moves.c: The pawn becomes a queen with check, and the new queen also attacks his rook on b2.
His king had to move, and your queen takes the rook.

steps.keyText: Queen with check if you can: he has no time to stop the new queen from doing more damage.

steps.setting: White to move. Your pawn on a7 is one step from queening, but his rook on c8 guards a8.

moves.c: Take his pawn on c2. If his rook takes back, it leaves the eighth rank and stops guarding a8.
Your pawn becomes a queen, and you have a queen against a rook.

steps.keyText: The piece guarding the queening square is the one to distract.

steps.setting: White to move. Your pawns on c6 and d6 are close to queening, and his king on e8 is near them.

moves.c: Check first: the king must step away from your pawns.
Now the pawn heads for c8, and his rook and knight cannot stop both pawns.

steps.keyText: When your pawns are close to queening, use checks to keep his king away from them.

tactics-check.title: Course exam
tactics-check.goal: Find the right pattern when nobody tells you which one it is.
tactics-check.rule: In every position run the same scan: checks, captures and threats, for both sides.
tactics-check.intro: In a game nobody tells you "this is a fork". So in this exam the patterns are mixed. Use one fixed scan in every position: first every check, then every capture, then every threat, and ask the same questions about his moves. The scan finds the tactic; the patterns you learned tell you what it is.

Both pawns become queens, but you have an extra rook.

courses.title: Think first
courses.sub: One short routine before every move, so that simple tactics stop costing you games.
courses.why: In your 175 analysed games, 31% of your mistakes were played in under 5 seconds. Your opponent's best answer to your mistake was a check 50 times, and you left a piece hanging 49 times. Most of these were easy to see: you did not look. This course builds one routine and trains it until it is automatic.

chapters.title: The routine
chapters.intro: Six short lessons. Each one adds one question to ask before you move. The cards come from your own games.

check3.title: The three questions
check3.goal: Stop leaving pieces where he can take them for free.
check3.rule: Before you let go of the piece, ask: after my move, what can he check, capture or threaten?
check3.intro: Most of your lost pieces were not deep tactics. Your opponent just took something, often with check. The cure is three quick questions about his next move, asked before you let go of the piece. Checks first, then captures, then threats. It takes ten seconds and you have ten minutes.

steps.setting: Your game against amirrezan, 7 Jan 2026. You played ((3...Bg4)) here after 3 seconds.

moves.c: Ask the questions about ((3...Bg4)) first. Check? No. Capture? Yes: ((3...Bg4 4.Qxg4)) and the bishop is gone. So take the pawn instead.
Now your knight challenges his knight.
Calm position, nothing hanging, and you still have both bishops.

steps.keyText: Before moving a piece, look at every enemy piece that could take it on its new square.

steps.setting: Your game against edipeca, 5 Mar 2026. White has just put his bishop on d3. You played ((4...c5)) after 5 seconds.

moves.c: His bishop attacks your bishop on f5, and nothing defends it. After ((4...c5 5.Bxf5)) your bishop is lost. The capture question would have saved it.
Your bishop is traded, not lost, and the position is level.

steps.keyText: When he attacks a piece, the capture question has an answer: move it, defend it or trade it.

hismove.title: What does his move want?
hismove.goal: Read his last move before you choose yours.
hismove.rule: Every move changes something: what does it attack now, and what did it stop defending?
hismove.intro: Your opponent's move is a message. Before you think about your plans, read it. Which piece moved? What does it attack from its new square? Which line did it open behind it? One look at his last move tells you most of his threats.

steps.setting: Your game against TheQueenSlayer19, 13 Aug 2026. You are White. Black takes your knight.

loose.title: Loose pieces drop off
loose.goal: Spot your undefended pieces before he does.
loose.rule: An undefended piece is a target for forks and double attacks: defend it or know why not.
loose.intro: A loose piece is one that nothing defends. On its own it is fine. But a fork or a check with a capture hits two things at once, and the loose one falls. Before you move, count your loose pieces. If one of them can be hit together with something else, fix that first.

checks.goal: See his checks before you move a piece away from your king.
checks.rule: List his checks before you move a piece away from your king or open a line.
checks.intro: In 50 of your mistakes, his best answer was a check. You must answer a check, so he gets a free move: to take a loose piece, bring another attacker or win time. Before you move, name every check he could give after your move. It takes five seconds.

gift.title: Is it a gift or a trap?
gift.goal: Punish his blunders, and do not fall for his bait.
gift.rule: When he leaves something, take ten seconds: usually it is a blunder, so punish it; sometimes it is bait.
gift.intro: Players at your level blunder often, so his mistakes are your best chance to win. When his move leaves something hanging, stop. Ask: can I take it, or hit two things at once? Then ask the three questions about your capture. If they come back clean, it was a gift: take it.

clock.title: Where your time should go
clock.goal: Spend your thinking time on the moves that decide the game.
clock.rule: Spend time when the position changes: captures, checks, pawn breaks, and whenever you are winning.
